name: Kxoe
sweep_summary: Kxoe/Khwe is not in the catalog. The single sweep item, Vossen 2003 'Verbal tone and stress in ǁAni', is about the sister language ǁAni [anii1246] (Glottolog links the reference to both codes; anii1246 is a separate language under the Kxoe subgroup). No open copy exists (Köppe sells the PDF; no DOI; archive.org/HathiTrust/Crossref/S2/OpenAlex gave nothing); Google Books snippet view (feed to automated fetch from the box) yielded the introduction: Vossen cites Heine (1999:18) that stress exists with unclear significance, on the last high-tone syllable preceded by a low tone, and says his own data show stress as a distinctive unit even in the verb's citation form; Downing 2010 (Survey of Word Accentual Patterns, p. 394, paywalled) summarises it as stress on the last High-toned syllable of verbs, with exceptions. The Vossen 1997 Druckakzent passage the earlier audit could not attribute is shown by a new snippet to concern ǁAni, not Kxoe. For Khwe proper the only first-hand stress statement reached is Kilian-Hatz 2008 (snippet): compound main stress on the first syllable of the first element with tonal sandhi; no source read states word-stress placement in simplex Khwe words, which remain described as three-tone. Acquisition priority: Kilian-Hatz 2008 (Harvard print) high; Vossen 2003 and Vossen 1997 p. 96 medium; Downing 2010 low. Receipts:, addendum, gbfeed/.

new_statements.quote: [Kilian-Hatz 2008, snippets:] first syllable of the first element takes the main stress of the compound and causes various tonal sandhi processes with regard to the following element. Generally, the second noun looses its original tone [...] stress is commonly, but not strictly lying on the first part of the [...] semantic part. In contrast, the classifier-like nouns and the derivative [...] nouns remain tonologically unchanged. Therefore, stress is not due to the slot in a nominal compound; it is rather observed on the main semantic part. [Haacke 1992:150:] Köhler in a recent publication (1989:112) reports that in Kxoé stress (Druckakzent) on the determiner influences the lexical tone of the compound.

Köln: Rüdiger Köppe (first-hand wording, Google Books snippets, pages not returned); corroborated second-hand by Haacke, W. H. G. 1992. The tonology of Khoekhoe (Nama/Damara). new_statements.locator: Kilian-Hatz 2008: nominal-compounding discussion (TOC 3.1.5 'Between nominal compounding and derivation: classifier-like nouns', pp. 89-96; snippet pages not shown). Haacke 1992: p. 150 (abbyy txt ll. 8001-8010).
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Khwe is a tone language (three lexical tones H/M/L; Kilian-Hatz 2003/2008, Chebanne 2007:448). Alongside tone the descriptions recognise a stress accent (Köhler's 'Druckakzent'): in nominal compounds the main stress falls on the first syllable of the first element as a rule, but it is really located on the semantically main element (usually but not strictly the first part), and the stressed element triggers tonal sandhi (the second noun loses its lexical tone). Vossen 1997 (snippet, language of passage not visible but apparently reporting Köhler on Kxoe) adds a verb-level pattern: some verbs carry stress on the [first] syllable in finite form, all others shift it to the following syllable; verbs of more than two syllables have main and secondary stress. No source opened gives a general rule for stress placement in simple words.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Vossen 1997 snippet: 'Mehr als zweisilbige Verben weisen Haupt- und Nebendruckakzent auf' (verbs of more than two syllables carry main and secondary stress) — attribution to Kxoe not verifiable from the snippet.
new_statements.exceptions: Compound stress is 'commonly, but not strictly' on the first element; classifier-like nouns and derivatives behave differently (remain tonologically unchanged); verbs split into a class with stem stress and a class that shifts stress to the following syllable (Vossen 1997 snippet).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern stress within nominal compounds (word level) and finite verb forms; interaction with lexical tone/sandhi is the focus. Kilian-Hatz 2008 describes the ǁXom Khwe dialect of West Caprivi (Namibia); Köhler's Kxoe data are from the same region (Mutc'iku). No phrase-level stress statement found.
new_statements.identity_note: Kilian-Hatz 2008 describes the ǁXom Khwe dialect of West Caprivi (Namibia), fieldwork 1997-2002; Köhler's Kxoe (1960s-80s, Mutc'iku, West Caprivi) is the same variety under its older name. Glottolog kxoe1243 covers all Khwe dialects (Buga, ǁXom, ǀGanda etc.). No separate dialect glottocode needed.

new_statements.reading: The only first-hand stress statement for Khwe proper reached in this sweep, and only as a snippet: in nominal compounds the main stress sits on the first syllable of the first (semantically main) element and drives tonal sandhi on the following element. It is a compound-prominence statement in a three-tone language, not a rule for word-stress placement in simplex words; no source read states where word stress falls in Khwe simplex words. For the sister language ǁAni (anii1246) Vossen 2003 (snippets) treats stress as a distinctive unit present even in the verb's citation form, summarised by Downing 2010 as 'assigned to the last High-toned syllable of verbs' with exceptions.

sources.citation: Haacke, Wilfrid H. G. 1992 [1993]. The tonology of Khoekhoe (Nama/Damara). PhD thesis, University College London (published 1999, Köppe).
sources.note: p. 150 (page number printed immediately before the passage; abbyy txt ll. 8001-8010): 'At this point it may be mentioned that Köhler in a recent publication (1989:112) reports that in Kxoé stress (Druckakzent) on the determiner influences the lexical tone of the compound. This phenomenon cannot be confirmed for Khoekhoe.' Second-hand report of Köhler 1989:112 on Kxoe; bibliography also lists Elderkin 1986 'Kxoe Tone and Kxoe Jonctures' (Contemporary Studies on Khoisan 1, Buske, pp. 225-235).
